title: BalancerPoolerV2.pool() and unlockCallback() lack nonReentrant — dispatch() sets the base-contract pattern but the new story-026 pool path skips it
rejectionNote: Severity-auditor + validity-checker: Two layers of third-party speculation about future Balancer V3 vault upgrades. Self-attested 'Not reachable against current Balancer V3 vault.' Root cause hypothetical and OOS.
description: ATokenDispatcherV2 already inherits OpenZeppelin ReentrancyGuard and applies `nonReentrant` to the base `dispatch` entry point. Story-026 added a second external entry point, `pool(uint256 minBPT)`, which synchronously hands control to the Balancer V3 vault (`IBalancerVault(_vault).unlock(data)`); the vault synchronously calls back into `unlockCallback`, which is gated only by `require(msg.sender == _vault)`. `pool` itself and `unlockCallback` both lack `nonReentrant`. Today the Balancer V3 unlock pattern is itself non-reentrant from the vault side, so re-entry is not reachable. But if the Balancer vault is later upgraded (proxy-based governance) or a future vault hook introduces a callback path that executes user-supplied code with msg.sender == vault (there are multiple such proposals in Balancer V3 hook extensions), the dispatcher's remaining defense against nested unlock cycles is only Balancer's own state machine. Inside `unlockCallback`, state reads (`IERC20(_sUSDS).balanceOf(address(this))` via the outer pool() read and the `vaultBefore`/`actualInVault` reads) and the `settle` call would be evaluated against potentially-stale state if re-entry ever became possible.
impact: No current exploit — depends on Balancer's non-reentrant behavior. The finding is defense-in-depth: the contract already pays the SLOAD cost of ReentrancyGuard for `dispatch`, the incremental cost is one extra SLOAD on pool() path. Gives the contract a per-function guarantee instead of relying on an external dependency's behavior.
attack_path: Not reachable against current Balancer V3 vault.

If vault is later upgraded to introduce a callback whose execution context still satisfies `msg.sender == _vault`, an attacker can sit on that callback, call pool() again mid-unlockCallback, and race the `sUSDSAmount` read / `settle` call against the nested state. Mitigation there depends entirely on Balancer fixing it on their side.
recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `pool(uint256 minBPT)` AND `unlockCallback(bytes calldata)`. Cost is effectively nil (reuses the existing ReentrancyGuard slot) and removes the contract's dependency on Balancer's internal reentrancy semantics.
dedupNote: Unique. Targets pool()/unlockCallback() entry points added by story-026 (decoupled pooling). Round-03 L-03 covers sandwich-on-pool() — different root cause (mempool MEV, not reentrancy). No prior round flags missing nonReentrant on these specific functions. Not covered by knownIssues.
sanitizeNote: In V2 focus area (story-026 pool()/unlockCallback() entry points). Not owner-driven (relies on hypothetical Balancer V3 vault upgrade). Defense-in-depth only — no current exploit. Lowest priority of the surviving Lows; consider folding into QA bundle. No match against project knownIssues.
classifyNote: C4 regular-audit Low/QA. Finding self-attests 'Not reachable against current Balancer V3 vault' — re-entry requires a hypothetical future Balancer vault upgrade introducing a callback whose execution context still satisfies msg.sender == _vault. Speculation on third-party future code, which C4 explicitly discourages. Lowest-impact of the five surviving Lows; recommend folding into the QA bundle as a single-line defense-in-depth observation rather than its own L-entry. Confirm Low.
validityNote: Filtered as known-invalid: speculation on third-party future code without demonstrated root cause. Finding self-attests 'Not reachable against current Balancer V3 vault' and the entire harm chain requires a hypothetical future Balancer vault upgrade introducing a callback that still satisfies msg.sender == _vault. Root cause (if it ever materializes) lives in Balancer's vault, which is out-of-scope third-party code. C4 explicitly discourages this pattern. Pure defense-in-depth with no present-day reachability and no in-scope root cause. Drop from submission; do not include in QA bundle as a standalone item.
